method: Each history is stated in plain terms, worked out on paper, and transcribed here. No figure in this file was produced by running this program. Every expected value carries the arithmetic that produced it, so a reader can check the number without trusting the code — deriving an expectation through the machinery under test proves only that it agrees with itself, which is what let the bugs these histories catch survive.
companies: Invented. Nothing here is a real security and nothing here is a recommendation. Real-company evidence lives only in tests/fixtures/groundtruth, where a hand-read figure can be checked against its filing.

conventions.clock: Every history is read live, on whatever day the suite runs. Every lot and every stored close is dated on or before 2026-08-07, so no figure here depends on the run date and none of them can drift.
conventions.returns: Percent numbers, rounded to 2 decimal places by the host. 17.5 means 17.5%.
conventions.weight: A percent number, unrounded by the host. Compared to 6 decimal places.
conventions.absent: null means the host must serve an absence. It must never serve 0, and never a figure carried over from anything else.
conventions.must_not_be: The answer the code gave, or would give, when the defect this history was built for is present. A history whose must_not_be is what comes back has caught a regression, not a rounding difference.

histories.why: The class held is not the class priced. Two symbols map to one CIK; the class the journal does not hold has the newer close, so a max-by-date pick across every mapped symbol takes it. Twenty shares of the cheap class then read as the dear one, and the error propagates into market value, the account total, and every weight measured against it.
story: Northwind Systems has two listed share classes. The SEC maps both NWND (Class A) and NWND.B (Class B) to CIK 700001.
This journal holds the Class B security, NWND.B.
On 2026-01-05, 20 shares of NWND.B were bought at $400.00 each.
The stored price history has NWND closing at $705,000.00 on 2026-08-07, and NWND.B closing at $470.00 on 2026-08-06.
The Class A close is one day newer. That is what makes the wrong answer win.
Free cash in this journal is $600.00.

position_return.how: one lot, so the lifetime figure is that lot's

return.how: one purchase in the period; same arithmetic as the lot

market_value.how: 20 x 705,000.00 — the Class A close against a Class B holding

price_ticker.how: the class the journal does not hold, chosen because its close was one day newer

value.how: 600.00 free cash + 9,400.00 of NWND.B at market

histories.why: Per-sale and per-period figures diverge, and they must both be right at once. Two sales out of one purchase: one up 50%, one down 25%, and the holding period they belong to up 5%. A layer that reported the period figure per sale, or averaged the sales into the period, would be plausible and wrong in both directions.

histories.why: Cash of nothing is an answer, not an absence, and an account on margin is a real account. The boundary is where the account reaches nothing: above it a weight is arithmetic however large, at or below it there is no share to express. None of the three may collapse into each other.

cash_cases.how: nothing in cash is a stated answer. The account is the holding alone, and the holding is all of it.
200.00 of an account of 1.00. Arithmetically true on margin and reported as it stands — the host holds no view that a weight cannot exceed 100.
the account works out to exactly nothing, so there is no share of it to express. Not a division by zero, and not 0%.
an account of less than nothing has no share to express
the cash question was never answered, so the account is absent for that reason — not because a price is missing

histories.why: A price typed into the journal is the only price for a security the SEC does not match, and it is the one price nobody validated. A positive one has to be used and labelled as undated; a price of nothing, or less than nothing, is not a price at all — served as one it produces a $0 market value, a 0% weight and a -100% on every open share, four confident answers resting on a claim the market never made.

histories.why: A holding period's return is built from its purchases. Rebuilding each purchase's money from its already-rounded percentage, and then dividing once more, is not the same arithmetic as adding up the money — and it lets a period report a figure its own lots do not add up to. Off in the last place only, which is exactly the kind of wrong number nobody notices.

histories.why: Shares that cost nothing and a sale that fetched nothing are real entries, not missing ones — but neither can stand for a price. A change measured from nothing has no value, and free shares say nothing about the market. Reporting either as a percentage would put a fabricated figure into the evidence that judges the sell rules, which is the one place it would be believed.
